2026 Reliability Technical Conference




Operational Challenges of Integrating Large Loads in Evolving System Dynamics
           Prepared for filing with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
            2026 Reliability Technical Conference: Docket No. AD26-8-000
                   Wayman L. Smith, American Electric Power (AEP)
                       on Behalf of the Edison Electric Institute
                                     October 13, 2026




                         Large Load and Grid Reliability Testimony | 1
                                                                           2026 Reliability Technical Conference

Introduction
The electric industry is entering a period of unprecedented change driven by the rapid growth of
large computational loads, accelerating deployment of inverter-based resources, evolving resource
adequacy challenges, and increasing interdependence among electric, fuel, communications, and
digital infrastructure systems. These developments are reshaping many of the assumptions that
have historically guided transmission planning, operational reliability assessments, interconnection
practices, and reliability standards.
The following responses discuss how utilities, system operators, regulators, and large-load
developers can adapt existing planning and operational frameworks to maintain reliability while
supporting economic growth and technological innovation. The discussion focuses on emerging
challenges associated with large energy-intensive loads, inverter-based resources, declining system
inertia, cybersecurity and physical security risks, fuel assurance, and evolving reliability
requirements, while identifying practical measures that can strengthen the reliability and resilience
of the Bulk Power System as these trends continue to accelerate.




                               Large Load and Grid Reliability Testimony | 2
                                                                               2026 Reliability Technical Conference

1. How should entities model and plan for the rapid emergence of large, energy-intensive loads,
such as data centers and AI compute campuses, whose scale, timing, and operational
characteristics challenge traditional interconnection, transmission planning, and resource
adequacy frameworks? What lessons have been learned from the integration of large loads?
The rapid growth of data centers, artificial intelligence compute campuses, cryptocurrency mining
operations, hydrogen production facilities, and other large energy-intensive loads requires an evolution in
transmission planning and reliability assessment. Unlike traditional commercial and industrial customers,
these facilities can develop rapidly, connect at unprecedented scale, rely heavily on power-electronic
equipment, and exhibit dynamic responses to grid disturbances that may materially affect bulk power system
reliability.
Historically, planning focused primarily on forecasting load growth and ensuring sufficient transmission
capacity to meet forecast demand. That approach is no longer sufficient. Entities must evaluate not only how
much load may connect, but also where and when it will develop, how credible the forecast is, how the facility
will operate under normal and abnormal conditions, how it will respond to disturbances, and how its
performance will be monitored and validated over time.
Forecasting and Planning
Planning processes should distinguish speculative requests from projects that demonstrate increasing levels
of commitment through site control, financial security, equipment procurement, executed agreements,
construction activity, and phased development milestones. Forecasts should include energization schedules,
ramp trajectories, load factors, operational flexibility, and the likelihood of reaching full buildout.
Planners should evaluate accelerated, delayed, reduced, and canceled development scenarios. At the same
time, planners should recognize that transmission infrastructure often requires substantially longer
development timelines than large-load facilities, creating a risk that load growth may outpace network
expansion if investments are delayed.
Area-wide assessments are increasingly important. Individual projects can exceed 1,000 MW and clusters of
facilities may collectively reach several gigawatts within a concentrated area. As a result, planning should
assess aggregate impacts on transmission flows, resource adequacy, system strength, stability, and
generation dispatch rather than evaluating each facility in isolation.
Dynamic Modeling and Reliability Studies
Large computational loads should not be represented solely as static demand assumptions. NERC's Large
Load Working Group has identified characteristics that distinguish these facilities from conventional load,
including rapid ramping, block loading and unloading, extensive use of power electronics, automated
responses to disturbances, operational flexibility, and the potential for common-mode behavior across
similar equipment.
Planning entities should obtain sufficient technical information to develop dynamic models that represent
the complete facility, including information technology equipment, uninterruptible power supply systems,
cooling equipment, protection systems, backup generation, battery energy storage systems, transfer logic,
and facility controls. The objective is not maximum model complexity, but sufficient fidelity to accurately
represent behaviors that may affect bulk power system reliability.
Reliability studies should evaluate a broad range of operating conditions, including peak and off-peak periods,
varying renewable output levels, transmission outages, resource adequacy stress conditions, weak-grid
conditions, low-inertia conditions, and scenarios involving simultaneous energization or operation of multiple
facilities.
Studies should also evaluate frequency stability, voltage stability, transient stability, oscillatory performance,
fault response, disturbance ride-through performance, interactions with inverter-based resources, and the

                                   Large Load and Grid Reliability Testimony | 3
                                                                              2026 Reliability Technical Conference

potential for common-mode load loss. Electromagnetic transient studies should be performed when power-
electronic interactions, fast controls, weak-grid conditions, or protection-system behavior cannot be
adequately represented using traditional positive-sequence models.
Importantly, planning should assess both load growth and rapid load-loss scenarios. The sudden loss of
several thousand megawatts of computational load may present reliability challenges comparable to the loss
of a major generation resource and should therefore be evaluated in both planning and operational
assessments.
Model Validation, Monitoring, and Operational Coordination
Experience has demonstrated that providing a model during the interconnection process is only the first step.
Models should be validated during commissioning and commercial operation by comparing measured facility
performance with modeled behavior. Validation should include voltage response, frequency response,
disturbance ride-through performance, protection-system operation, load recovery characteristics, and the
behavior of backup generation and storage systems.
Appropriate disturbance monitoring should be installed at key points of interconnection to support event
reconstruction, root-cause analysis, performance verification, and model validation. Where conventional
telemetry is insufficient, higher-resolution monitoring may be necessary to capture rapid load changes,
transfer events, protection actions, and other power-electronic behaviors.
Entities should also establish requirements for notification of material changes in facility size, configuration,
operating characteristics, controls, equipment, backup generation, or energy storage systems so that
reliability assessments remain accurate throughout the life of the project.
Performance Requirements and Reliability Expectations
Industry experience has also highlighted the need for clear and enforceable performance requirements.
Interconnection requirements should address voltage and frequency ride-through capabilities, protection-
system coordination, disturbance response, recovery characteristics, permissible disconnection behavior,
reactive power performance, model submission and validation obligations, disturbance monitoring, event
reporting, and qualified-change notification requirements.
Operational coordination should continue after a facility enters service. Transmission providers, balancing
authorities, reliability coordinators, and large-load operators should maintain visibility into load levels,
operating modes, commissioning schedules, outage plans, operational flexibility, and expected responses to
system events and operator instructions.
Evolving Reliability Framework
The reliability framework governing large computational loads continues to evolve. NERC's Project 2026-02
is intended to establish foundational requirements addressing interconnection, studies, modeling data, and
coordination responsibilities. In parallel, NERC's Large Load Working Group has identified additional reliability
gaps involving ride-through performance, model validation, disturbance monitoring, planning for large-load
loss, and operational reliability assessments.
Entities should not wait for every national requirement to become effective before addressing known
reliability risks. Where appropriate, planning authorities and transmission providers should incorporate
technically justified modeling, monitoring, validation, performance, and coordination requirements into their
study practices, tariffs, service agreements, interconnection procedures, and operating requirements.
Large computational loads should not be viewed simply as larger versions of traditional customer demand.
Their scale, pace of development, power-electronic characteristics, operational flexibility, and disturbance-
response behavior create unique planning and operational challenges. A prudent framework therefore
requires credible forecasting, planning, dynamic facility modeling, fit-for-purpose stability studies,
commissioning and operational model validation, disturbance monitoring, ongoing operational coordination,

                                  Large Load and Grid Reliability Testimony | 4
                                                                              2026 Reliability Technical Conference

and enforceable performance requirements. By incorporating these elements into planning and operations,
the industry can support economic development while maintaining the reliability and resilience of the bulk
electric system.


2. ERCOT is proposing to require advanced grid support functions (e.g., fast-frequency response
and synthetic inertia) for future BESS in response to reliability events and operational trends such
as frequency excursions, voltage instability, and IBR-driven oscillations. Are these same issues
present elsewhere, and should similar requirements be applied nationwide?
Yes. In my opinion, future battery energy storage systems (BESS) should be required to possess advanced
grid-support capabilities nationwide, while planners and operators retain flexibility to determine when and
how those capabilities are deployed.
The reliability challenges driving ERCOT's Advanced Grid Support requirements are not unique to Texas. As
inverter-based resources become a larger share of generation across the United States, many regions are
experiencing declining system strength, reduced contributions from synchronous resources, changing
frequency-response characteristics, voltage-stability concerns, and increasingly complex inverter-control
interactions.
ERCOT has addressed these concerns through NOGRR 272, which establishes Advanced Grid Support
requirements for inverter-based Energy Storage Resources. Importantly, ERCOT's framework is performance-
based rather than technology-prescriptive. It focuses on the ability of a resource to provide grid-support
functionality under a range of system conditions without mandating a specific inverter design or control
architecture. This distinction is important because reliability requirements should define the performance
needed by the system rather than prescribe a particular technology solution.
Other regions are reaching similar conclusions. MISO's system-attributes work found that grid-forming
controls can improve voltage-stability limits and provide services historically supplied by synchronous
machines. MISO is also developing system-strength screening methodologies to identify areas where inverter
interactions may create reliability concerns. Similarly, SPP has increased its focus on inverter-based resource
modeling, performance testing, and model validation to ensure converter-based resources can be accurately
represented in reliability assessments.
Advanced grid-support functions may also help address oscillatory stability concerns. Research has shown
that appropriately designed BESS controls can contribute to damping subsynchronous resonance and
subsynchronous control interactions that may arise from interactions among inverter controls, synchronous
machines, and series-compensated transmission facilities. While this issue is particularly relevant in some
regions, including ERCOT, it illustrates a broader trend toward utilizing inverter-based resources to support
overall system stability.
For these reasons, new BESS installations should be capable of providing advanced grid-support functions
such as:
    •   Grid-forming or equivalent advanced grid-support performance;
    •   Fast frequency and inertia-like response;
    •   Dynamic voltage support;
    •   Stable operation in low-system-strength conditions;
    •   Robust disturbance ride-through;
    •   Oscillation-damping capability where technically justified; and
    •   Validated models demonstrating required performance.

However, a nationwide framework should distinguish between requiring capability and requiring continuous
deployment. The value of inertia-like response, voltage support, system-strength contribution, oscillation
damping, and other advanced functions varies substantially based on system topology, resource mix,
operating conditions, and electrical location. Planners and operators should therefore retain flexibility to
determine which functions are needed, where they should be enabled, and what level of performance is
required.


3. How should operators quantify and manage the reliability implications of declining system
inertia in regions with rapid interconnection of large loads and where IBR penetration is
accelerating and replacing conventional generation?
Declining synchronous inertia increases the rate of change of frequency following major disturbances and
reduces the time available for responsive resources to arrest frequency decline. As a result, operators can no
longer rely solely on traditional capacity-based reliability metrics. Instead, reliability assessments should
incorporate explicit frequency-security metrics that account for inertia, contingency size, response capability,
protection settings, and large-load behavior.
Operators should evaluate not only total system inertia, but also locational characteristics that influence
frequency performance. Important measures include total and locational synchronous inertia, the largest
credible loss of generation, load, or transfer capability, expected rate of change of frequency (RoCoF),
frequency nadir, settling frequency, available primary and fast frequency response, and the performance of
underfrequency and overfrequency protection systems. NERC has consistently identified inertia, contingency
magnitude, and response speed as key drivers of frequency performance, while ERCOT has developed
operational tools and critical-inertia methodologies to monitor these risks in real time.
Managing reliability in a lower-inertia grid requires a combination of forecasting, operational awareness, and
responsive resources. Operators should forecast inertia and available frequency response in both day-ahead
and real-time timeframes, establish study-based operating limits where appropriate, and ensure sufficient
responsive capability is available to arrest frequency excursions following credible contingencies. Depending
on system conditions, this may include committing synchronous resources or synchronous condensers,
procuring fast frequency response, and leveraging advanced capabilities from inverter-based resources.
Large loads should also be incorporated into frequency-security assessments. As large computational loads
become increasingly significant components of system demand, planners and operators should understand
how these facilities are expected to respond during disturbances and ensure that ride-through requirements
and protection settings do not contribute to unnecessary or cascading load-loss events. Likewise, regions
with high penetrations of inverter-based resources may require grid-forming controls, system-strength
mitigation measures, or other solutions identified through stability and EMT studies.
Ultimately, maintaining frequency reliability in a lower-inertia system requires a shift from simple capacity-
based assessments to a more comprehensive evaluation of frequency security. Reliability assessments should
explicitly consider inertia, contingency size, response capability, protection-system performance, and the
behavior of both generation and large loads. This provides a more complete measure of system resilience
and enables operators to proactively manage emerging reliability risks as the resource mix continues to
evolve.

4. What are the primary cybersecurity and physical security risks associated with integrating large
loads onto the grid? Which risks are unique to specific types of large loads (e.g., data centers,
crypto mining, industrial loads)? How is industry addressing cybersecurity and physical security
risks posed by large loads?
The integration of large computational loads and other high-density electric consumers introduces both
traditional critical infrastructure risks and new reliability concerns. As these facilities become larger and more
concentrated, their potential impact on Bulk Power System (BPS) reliability increases, particularly if load
behavior can change rapidly or be remotely controlled.
Reliability Risks Unique to Specific Large Load Types
Data Centers and AI/Computational Loads
    •   Extremely large and rapidly growing demand concentrations.
    •   High penetration of power-electronic-based equipment that can exhibit complex dynamic
        performance during grid disturbances.
    •   Potential for coordinated control of thousands of servers and cooling systems, enabling rapid load
        reductions or increases.
    •   Increasing use of behind-the-meter generation and battery storage systems that may not be fully
        visible to planners and operators.
Cryptocurrency Mining Facilities
    •   Ability to rapidly curtail or reconnect large portions of load within seconds or minutes.
    •   Highly automated operational controls.
    •   Economic incentives that can result in frequent operational changes tied to market conditions.
Large Industrial Loads
    •   Complex operational processes that may be sensitive to voltage and frequency disturbances.
    •   Potential safety, environmental, and equipment damage consequences if operations are disrupted.
    •   Large motor loads that can significantly affect system recovery following disturbances.
Industry is increasingly adopting measures focused on visibility, planning, operational preparedness, and
security requirements, including:
    •   Enhanced interconnection studies evaluating load dynamics, voltage performance, frequency
        response, and disturbance ride-through characteristics.
    •   Improved modeling requirements for large loads, including disclosure of behind-the-meter
        generation, energy storage, and controllable load capabilities.
    •   Expanded disturbance monitoring and event analysis programs to better understand large-load
        behavior during system events.
    •   Development of NERC reliability guidance, Large Load Task Force recommendations, and proposed
        standards that address planning, modeling, and operational considerations for large loads.
    •   Increased coordination among transmission planners, balancing authorities, reliability coordinators,
        and large-load operators.
    •   Physical security best practices and assessments for critical substations and interconnection facilities.
As large computational loads become increasingly capable of materially affecting Bulk Power System
reliability, a strong case exists that these facilities should be subject to cybersecurity requirements
                                   Large Load and Grid Reliability Testimony | 7
                                                                             2026 Reliability Technical Conference

comparable to the NERC Critical Infrastructure Protection (CIP) standards when their size, operational
characteristics, or ability to affect grid reliability reach defined thresholds.
Applying NERC CIP requirements, or a comparable regulatory framework, would provide several reliability
benefits:
    •   Establish minimum cybersecurity controls for systems capable of materially affecting bulk power
        system operations.
    •   Require asset identification, access control, monitoring, incident response, recovery planning, and
        supply chain risk management.
    •   Reduce the risk that a cyber compromise could trigger load changes with reliability consequences.
    •   Improve visibility into critical cyber assets associated with large loads and behind-the-meter
        resources.
    •   Create a more consistent security framework between reliability-critical generation, transmission
        assets, and large loads capable of producing comparable system impacts.
As large computational loads increasingly provide demand response, utilize grid-support technologies,
control large behind-the-meter energy resources, or represent gigawatt-scale demand concentrations,
applying CIP-based cybersecurity requirements becomes an important consideration for maintaining bulk
system reliability and resilience. Such requirements would help ensure that entities capable of materially
affecting grid operations are held to cybersecurity standards commensurate with their reliability impact.


5. How do utilities account for the interaction of behind-the-meter gas-fired generators compared
to front-of-meter gas-fueled power generators on the same pipeline in planning and operations?
Behind-the-meter gas-fired generation may reduce metered electric demand, but it often relies on the same
gas production, transportation, compression, storage, and delivery infrastructure that serves front-of-meter
generation. As a result, evaluating only net electric load can understate common-mode fuel-supply risks and
overstate the reliability benefits of onsite generation.
To properly assess these interactions, utilities, pipelines, generators, and large-load customers should
develop a common view of fuel demand that incorporates both front-of-meter and behind-the-meter gas
consumption under normal, contingency, islanded, and emergency operating conditions. Studies should
evaluate aggregate gas demand by pipeline segment and delivery point, contractual fuel arrangements,
compressor dependencies, pressure constraints, storage availability, dual-fuel capability, and the potential
for coincident operation of onsite and grid-supplied generation.
Reliability assessments should also test conditions that could stress both the electric and gas systems
simultaneously, including extreme weather events, pipeline outages, compressor failures, and periods when
onsite and front-of-meter resources are operating at high output. Particular attention should be given to
avoiding double-counting behind-the-meter generation as both a load reduction and an independent
reliability resource unless fuel availability, deliverability, controls, and operating authority have been
demonstrated.
Operational coordination is equally important. Dispatch priorities, curtailment protocols, and emergency
procedures should be structured so that operation of onsite generation does not unintentionally reduce fuel
availability for front-of-meter resources needed to maintain bulk-system reliability.
In short, behind-the-meter gas generation should be evaluated as part of the broader gas-electric system
rather than solely as a reduction in electric load. Reliability assessments should explicitly consider shared
pipeline dependencies, fuel deliverability constraints, contractual firmness, compressor dependencies, and

coincident operation with front-of-meter generation to ensure onsite resources strengthen, rather than
inadvertently degrade, system reliability.


6. How should capacity and fuel assurance evolve for high-load-factor data centers?
High-load-factor data centers can flatten the load-duration curve and increase the number of hours during
which dependable energy production is required. As a result, resource adequacy can no longer be evaluated
solely on whether sufficient installed capacity exists during seasonal peak conditions. Planning must also
consider whether accredited resources can reliably produce energy through prolonged periods of system
stress.
AEP addresses this challenge by focusing on both capacity adequacy and fuel assurance. For natural gas
generation, AEP evaluates fuel-supply risks in both planning and operations and seeks firm transportation
arrangements where appropriate. As data center growth increases system load factors, AEP supports
resource adequacy approaches that evaluate the ability of resources to reliably deliver energy throughout
extended stress events, not just during peak-demand hours.
More broadly, resource adequacy frameworks should evolve toward an energy-assurance construct that
integrates capacity accreditation, fuel security, resource duration, and transmission deliverability. Utilities
and RTOs/ISOs should assess multi-hour and multi-day energy sufficiency; accredit resources based on
demonstrated performance during correlated weather, fuel, and transmission disruptions; evaluate natural
gas pipeline and storage constraints, including common-mode fuel dependencies; and account for the
duration limits, recharge requirements, and correlated performance of energy-limited resources. These
assessments should be supported by seasonal stress testing, extreme-weather scenarios, and probabilistic
resource adequacy analysis.
Large-load flexibility may provide additional reliability value where tariffs and operating frameworks permit,
but it should not replace firm reliability planning unless the capability is measurable, dispatchable, and
enforceable. Similarly, behind-the-meter generation should only be credited as a reliability contribution
when fuel availability, interconnection arrangements, environmental constraints, testing requirements, and
operating characteristics demonstrate that the resource can perform as expected during system stress.
In short, the industry should move beyond a framework focused primarily on peak capacity and adopt a
broader assessment of energy assurance. Reliability evaluations should consider accredited capacity, fuel
security, transmission deliverability, resource duration, and performance during extended stress conditions
to ensure the system can meet growing demand from high-load-factor customers while maintaining
reliability.

Conclusion
The common thread across these questions is that large loads must become active participants in reliability
planning rather than passive consumers of grid service. FERC, NERC, RTOs/ISOs, transmission providers,
utilities, and customers should establish a coordinated framework that includes:
   1. Validated steady-state, dynamic, and EMT models where appropriate.
   2. Enhanced interconnection and commissioning requirements.
   3. Disturbance monitoring, event reporting, and operational telemetry.
   4. Ride-through, protection coordination, and qualified-change controls.
   5. Performance-based essential reliability services from inverter-based resources.
   6. Explicit inertia, frequency-security, and system-strength assessment.
   7. Cybersecurity and physical-security obligations proportionate to reliability impact.
   8. Gas-electric coordination and fuel- and energy-assurance analysis.
This framework is consistent with the direction of NERC's Large Loads Action Plan, its developing
computational-load standards, FERC's recent large-load actions, ERCOT's technical work, and broader
RTO/ISO efforts to adapt interconnection and reliability practices.
